table.brief: Two sibling sub-columns under "Price" where one holds short numbers ($12) and the other long qualifiers ("$12 per seat per month, billed annually")

understanding.purpose: A plan-comparison price sheet: the reader first identifies a plan, then reads across to see what it costs, what the billing commitment is, and what operational constraints (seats, contract, support) come with it.
understanding.reading: Mostly row-wise: the eye anchors on the Plan name, jumps to the Price block (list price then the billing sentence that explains it), then continues right to the short fact columns (seats, contract, support) which are scanned vertically for comparison between plans. Column 3 is prose, not a value; columns 2/4/5/6 are short comparable facts.
groups: cols 1 alone — row identity, the entry point for every scan
cols 2–3 — one merged 'Price' header; the number and its terms must be adjacent and read together
cols 4–6 — short constraint/support facts of equal role, read as a small comparable block
col 2 vs cols 4–6 — numeric/short tokens that benefit from tight, uniform widths
keep_intact: Plan names, especially 'Enterprise' (75px, must not break)
'List price' and 'Billing terms' as word units (no mid-word breaks)
'Minimum seats', 'Contract', 'Support' as word units in the header
dollar amounts ($12, $45) and figures like 250+ in the billing text
may_wrap: Billing terms sentence in col 3 (longest, 490px one-line — the natural place to absorb height)

preferred.name: r3B
preferred.note: Refines r2C: keep the one-line List price header at 88 and Billing at 212; take 10px from Contract (100 to 90) and give it to Support (122 to 132). Contract still wraps to two lines, while Support now holds Team and Education on two lines. This keeps the compact header and reduces r2C's right-side cramping without widening the table.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: A different balance point: treat the three fact columns as a compact equal-role block (92/92/122) and push the extra width into the billing sentence (240px), which is the only cell that legitimately needs to wrap. Minimum seats at 92 still fits '25' and wraps its header to two lines; Support at 122 keeps 'Dedicated success manager' and 'Community forum and email' at two lines. Aims for a 2–3 line billing block and a much shorter table than r0C.

acceptable.name: r1C
acceptable.note: A near-uniform short-fact rhythm: Minimum seats 88 (67px text — just enough for 'Minimum' so the header wraps to two balanced lines), Contract 100, Support 124, with billing at 232 as the only wide prose column and List price at 66 (two-line header, as in r0A). Tests whether giving the numeric column the tightest defensible width and spending the savings on billing produces the shortest table without splitting any word.

acceptable.name: r2A
acceptable.note: Take the 8px of dead space off Minimum seats (88→88 kept as the floor, Contract kept at 100) and pull 10px out of the price number column (66→60, header already wraps there) to push Support from 124 to 136px. At ~115px of text every support entry ('Dedicated success manager', 'Community forum and email', 'Email and chat, 8h response') drops to two lines, so Support stops driving row height and Billing becomes the only column that ever needs a third line. Billing still gets 226px (≈205px of text), so most sentences stay at two lines and the ragged 60/83 rhythm is reduced to just the genuinely long plans.

acceptable.name: r2B
acceptable.note: Tests the opposite priority: give the prose column everything left over (244px → 223px of text) so the long Business, Enterprise and Nonprofit sentences fall back to two lines, and accept Support at 118px (97px of text) where the longest two entries take three lines. The point is to see whether killing the 3-line billing rows shortens the table more than the extra support wrapping costs — Support entries are short facts, so a third line there reads as a natural sentence break, whereas a third line in Billing lengthens the whole row.

acceptable.name: r2C
acceptable.note: The unexplored alternative: spend 28px on col 2 so 'List price' sits on one line and the Price subheader row collapses to a single clean line aligned with 'Billing terms', which also removes the broken 'List / price' element seen in all three renders. Because the header block is currently sized by the two-line subheader, this saves roughly a line of header height — about the same as one extra three-line row — while making the most-scanned part of the table tidier. Billing drops to 212px (191px of text), which is the deliberate cost of the test.

acceptable.name: r3A
acceptable.note: Refines r2A: keep Plan 96, List 60, Billing 224 and Seats 88; move 6px from Contract (100 to 94) and 8px to Support (136 to 144), with Billing down 2px. Support now fits 'success manager' on one line, so Enterprise and Education support descriptions become two lines; Contract still breaks into two lines but is less cramped; Billing remains wide enough for Education to stay at two lines.

acceptable.name: r3C
acceptable.note: Refines r2B by narrowing Contract 100 to 90 and widening Support 118 to 132, taking the extra 4px from Billing 244 to 240. Billing gets the most prose room of the List-60 designs, Support stops forcing Team and Education into three lines, and Contract remains two-line; the table avoids r2B's 570px height.

bad.name: contrast
bad.note: This equalizes the two Price subcolumns and overpays the short List price column while starving Billing terms, the only long prose column. Billing terms would wrap to 4–5 lines in most rows, making the table tall and ragged, while Support is unnecessarily wide.
bad.why: This equalizes the two Price subcolumns and overpays the short List price column while starving Billing terms, the only long prose column. Billing terms would wrap to 4–5 lines in most rows, making the table tall and ragged, while Support is unnecessarily wide.

rationale: Billing terms is the only true prose column, so it should dominate, but not at the cost of forcing the List price header to wrap. r3B gives List price exactly one-line header width, keeps Billing terms at 212px, and uses the remaining width for Support and Contract. Plan at 96px is the hard minimum for “Enterprise,” while Minimum seats and Contract can wrap without harming scanability. The result is 524px tall, with no cell over three lines and a clean two-row Price header.

general: Allocate width by content role and line-break cost, not by equal columns or symmetry.
A column’s hard floor is its longest unbreakable word plus padding; header wrapping is usually cheaper than wrapping every data cell.
Group headers such as Price should not force equal subcolumn widths; subcolumns should follow their own content.
Consistent row rhythm and avoiding 4+ line cells matter more than saving a few pixels in the header.
specific: List price needs 88px for a one-line header; 60px only wraps the header and is acceptable if Billing terms needs the space.
Billing terms at 212px keeps all billing strings to three lines or fewer; below about 204px some rows gain a line.
Support at 132px is the threshold that keeps “Email and chat, 8h response” to two lines; 122px makes it three.
Contract can be 90px and let “Monthly or annual” wrap; Minimum seats at 88px wraps its header harmlessly.

tradeoffs: r3B versus r3A/r3C is the real tradeoff: r3B spends 28px to keep “List price” on one line and the subheader row at 36px, while r3A/r3C give that width to Billing and Support, reducing some three-line cells but making the subheader row 60px. Both total 524px; the choice depends on whether a clean header or less ragged prose matters more.
uncertain: Whether the 88px List price column is worth it when its values are only “$12”–“$45”; some designers would choose 60px and accept the two-line header. Also whether Support at 132px versus 144px is worth the width, since Enterprise support remains three lines at 132px.

critique.good: Plan at 96px keeps 'Enterprise' on one line, and the 281px billing column reads comfortably in 2 lines for every plan, so the price sentence never fragments. The three fact columns are clearly a block on the right.
critique.problems: The table is uniformly 83px per body row — every row is as tall as its worst cell, so short facts like '1' or 'Annual only' sit in vast vertical space. 'List price' is squeezed to two stacked lines in a 58px column, 'Monthly or annual' breaks over three lines, and Support breaks over three to four lines. Overall the table is bloated at 593px for content that mostly needs two lines.
critique.cause: 58px in col 2 leaves exactly 37px of text — the bare minimum for 'price', so the header cannot sit on one line; 84px in col 5 (63px text) cannot hold 'Monthly or annual' (123px) on one line and forces 3 lines; 100px in col 6 (79px text) forces 3–4 lines in Support. Meanwhile 281px in col 3 is more than the billing text needs (2 lines everywhere), so ~60px of slack is wasted on the one column that could have absorbed nothing more.

critique.good: The most balanced of the three: reallocating width from billing to the fact columns drops the tallest cell from 4–5 lines to 4 only in the worst row, 'Minimum seats' and 'Contract' now read cleanly in two lines, and Plan at 100px is safe. Row heights vary honestly with content (60/83/106) instead of being padded to a uniform 83.
critique.problems: The billing column at 200px is now the bottleneck: the Enterprise and Nonprofit sentences break to four lines and create 106px rows that break the vertical rhythm, while the row above is only 60px. The eye sees a sawtooth down the price block. Col 4 at 115px (94px text) still wraps 'Minimum seats' onto two lines even though the only values in it are '1'–'25'.
critique.cause: 200px in col 3 gives 179px of text for a 490px sentence, so the longest billing terms need 4 lines; the 115px in col 4 is wasted on a column whose content is two characters wide, and 110px in col 5 still costs a 2-line wrap. Width is sitting in the cheap columns and missing from the expensive one.

critique.good: Billing terms are still legible and 'Minimum seats' finally fits on one header line; Plan at 110px is generous and every row header reads as a unit. No mid-word splits anywhere.
critique.problems: Too tall: 733px with rows of 106 and 129px. Billing sentences fragment into 5 lines — '$15 per seat per month, billed annually; 40% nonprofit discount applied' becomes a stack of short lines, which is exactly the kind of prose you want to read as two or three flowing lines. Contract and Support get 120/124px they do not need. The table looks like a narrow newspaper column on the left and airy empty columns on the right.
critique.cause: 160px in col 3 (139px text) is far below what a 490px sentence needs, so line count explodes to 5 and every row grows; the 110/130/120/124px in cols 1/4/5/6 are over-provisioned relative to their content (75px names, 2-character numbers, ~120px phrases), so the deficit in col 3 is paid for entirely in height.

critique.good: The shortest table of the three (547px) because fewer rows reach three lines. Contract at 100px is the widest of the three, so 'Monthly or annual' breaks into two balanced lines rather than three, and Support at 127px holds most entries in two lines. Plan column at 96px is exactly the 'Enterprise' floor and stays intact.
critique.problems: The Price subheader block looks broken: 'List price' is split into 'List' / 'price' while 'Billing terms' sits on a single line, so the two subheaders no longer read as a pair. Contract is just under its one-line threshold, so the two-word value 'Annual only' is broken across two lines in four rows — a short token wrapped for no reason while other columns have slack. Billing is the narrowest of the three (194px of text), so the three longest sentences take three lines while the short ones take two, giving a jagged 60/83 row rhythm.
critique.cause: 68px to col 2 gives only 47px of text (needs ~88px for 'List price' on one line) and 127px to col 6; both are taken out of col 3 (215px). Col 5 at 100px yields 79px of text, about 2px short of what 'Annual only' needs.

critique.good: The most generous billing column (240px → 219px of text), so the prose reads most evenly and the price block clearly dominates where it should. Minimum seats at 92px keeps its header on two clean lines and the tiny numeric values well spaced. No mid-word splits.
critique.problems: 'List price' is squeezed into 43px of text and splits badly, making the header the most awkward element on the page. Contract at 92px (71px of text) breaks 'Annual only' onto two lines in four rows. Support at 122px (101px of text) pushes 'Email and chat, 8h response' and 'Community forum and email' to three lines, so Support now competes with Billing in dictating row height — five rows at 83px and the tallest table of the three (570px).
critique.cause: The 240px given to col 3 and the 122px to col 6 leave col 5 below its ~101px one-line threshold and col 2 far below the ~88px needed for 'List price'; col 4 at 92px also overshoots its 66px unbreakable-word floor without buying anything.

critique.good: The most balanced of the three and the best starting point: Contract at 100px keeps 'Annual only' on one line (only the genuinely longer 'Monthly or annual' wraps, which is natural), Minimum seats at 88px wraps its header neatly over two lines, billing at 232px reads comfortably, and there are no mid-word splits.
critique.problems: Support is still the weak column: 124px gives 103px of text, so 'Community forum and email' and 'Email and chat, 8h response' break into three lines and pull five rows up to 83px. 'List price' still splits into two lines. The 88px on Minimum seats buys nothing over 87px, and the 8px of slack that would have been available is not enough to matter.
critique.cause: Col 6 needs roughly 136px (≈115px of text) to hold every support entry in two lines, but it is starved because col 3 at 232px and col 4 at 88px consume the budget; col 2 at 66px is also 22px below the one-line 'List price' threshold.

critique.good: Plan is protected at 96px, Billing gets 226px so most rows are only two lines, Support is wider than in r2B, and there are no mid-word splits.
critique.problems: The List price column is visibly starved: 'List price' splits over two lines and the column has much more header than value. Support still breaks 'Dedicated success manager' and 'Community forum and email' awkwardly, Contract wraps 'Annual only', and row heights are uneven because Billing and Support each hit three lines in different rows.
critique.cause: List price is 60px (39px content) against a 67px one-line header. Support is 136px (115px content), just under the width needed for 'success manager' on one line. Contract is 100px (79px content), just under 'Annual only' at about 80px. Billing at 226px still cannot hold the longest sentences in two lines.

critique.good: Billing is the widest at 244px, so its line breaks are more even; the uniform 83px data rows give a calm, regular rhythm; Plan and Minimum seats remain intact.
critique.problems: Support is the weak column: 118px forces Team, Enterprise and Education into three lines and makes every data row 83px tall, even rows whose Billing text is only two lines. The table is the tallest at 570px, with excess white space in Plan, List price, seats and Contract. List price is still a two-line header and Contract still wraps 'Annual only'.
critique.cause: Support at 118px (97px content) is far below the roughly 140px needed for two-line support descriptions. Billing at 244px still leaves the longest sentences at three lines, so the uniform 83px row height is driven by the narrow Support column. List price at 60px and Contract at 100px repeat r2A's header/value fits.

critique.good: List price at 88px gives a clean one-line 'List price' header and a compact 36px subheader; the header hierarchy is the clearest of the three, and Plan and Seats are protected with no mid-word splits.
critique.problems: Billing is squeezed to 212px, producing three-line prose for Business, Enterprise, Education and Nonprofit and an awkward '12- / month' hyphen break. Support at 122px forces Team and Education into three lines. Contract still wraps 'Annual only'. The Price block feels cramped while the List price column has surplus white space under the short dollar values.
critique.cause: Billing at 212px (191px content) is below the roughly 226px that lets Education sit on two lines and far below the longest sentences. Support at 122px (101px content) is below the roughly 126px needed for 'Email and chat,' and 132px for 'forum and email'. Contract at 100px (79px content) is just under 'Annual only'; List price at 88px (67px content) exactly fits its one-line header but is wider than its values require.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

ref_equal.why: Billing terms is the longest content but gets a narrow column, wrapping into 5–7 lines and making rows very tall; Support is over-wide with dead space, so proportions and scanning rhythm fail.

ref_auto.why: Billing terms is generously wide and rows stay compact, but the 'List price' header wraps awkwardly and Support is squeezed narrower than Contract despite longer text.

r1B.why: Billing terms gets the dominant share and headers mostly fit, but Support is narrower than Contract and wraps into three-line stacks, slightly weakening comparison.

r3B.why: Best balance: Billing terms remains clearly widest, Support is wider than Contract and wraps less, List price header fits, and the shorter columns stay proportionate.

r1C.why: Very close to the best: Billing terms is well served, but Support remains slightly narrower than Contract and some support cells still stack into three lines.

contrast.why: Billing terms is starved while List price, Contract and Support are over-wide, producing excessive wrapping and tall, uneven rows.

raw.unsure: C, D and E are close and exact rendered widths are hard to measure; the choice depends on whether Billing terms width or reduced Support wrapping matters more.

r3B.why: The long Billing terms column gets the widest share, Plan and List price stay intact, and the short columns remain compact; rows scan cleanly and the table uses nearly the full measure.

contrast.why: Billing terms is squeezed into 4–6 lines while Plan and List price have conspicuous empty space; rows become tall and ragged, so the table is slow to compare.

r1C.why: Billing terms has enough width for mostly 2–3 line rows, but “List price” is forced onto two lines and the table leaves a large unused right margin, weakening the Price group.

r1B.why: List price stays on one line and Billing terms remains readable at 2–3 lines; the hierarchy is clear, though unused width at the right could have enlarged the long text column.

ref_auto.why: Billing terms is too narrow, pushing Team/Business/Enterprise to four lines while Support and the short columns have spare room; readable but unnecessarily tall and uneven.

ref_equal.why: Billing terms is crushed into 5–8 lines; the main descriptive column dominates vertically while short columns waste width, making row comparison laborious.

raw.unsure: Exact column widths are inferred from the renders; C/D/E differ only subtly, and I am unsure whether the unused right-hand space in C–F is intentional.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
